title: Shares & dividends
examples: What is the difference between face value and market value?
How do I calculate the dividend yield for a company?
If I buy shares, what is the dividend I can expect?

explain.say: Today we learn about buying shares in a company. Shares represent a small piece of ownership in that business. Think of it like owning a tiny part of a big pie.
The face value is the official printed value of a share. It is what the company originally sets the share's worth at. For example, a share might have a face value of one unit.

The market value is what people are actually willing to pay for the share today. This price changes every day based on how well the company is doing. If the company does well, the market value usually goes up.

A dividend is a payment made to shareholders from the company's profits. The dividend yield tells you the dividend payment as a percentage of the current market price. We calculate it by dividing the annual dividend by the market price.
Let us look at a concrete example to see this in action. Suppose a share has a market value of ten units. If the company pays a dividend of one unit, the dividend yield is one tenth, or ten percent.

faq.q: What is the difference between face value and market value?
faq.a: The face value is the fixed, original value printed on the share certificate. The market value is the fluctuating price you buy or sell the share for today.
asks: Is the face value always the same?

faq.q: Does a high dividend yield always mean a good investment?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A high yield might mean the share price has dropped a lot, which could signal problems with the company. You must look at other factors too.
asks: Should I only look at the yield?

faq.q: How often are dividends paid out?
faq.a: Companies decide how often to pay dividends. Some pay them quarterly, while others might pay them annually or even irregularly.
asks: Is there a set schedule for dividends?

faq.q: If the company makes no profit, will there be a dividend?
faq.a: No, companies generally cannot pay dividends if they have not made a profit. Dividends come directly from the company's earnings.
asks: What if the company loses money?

faq.q: Does the face value affect how much dividend I get?
faq.a: No, the face value does not directly determine the dividend amount. The board of directors decides the dividend based on profits, not the face value.
asks: Is face value important for dividends?
Does the printed value matter for payouts?

facts: Shares represent fractional ownership in a company.
The market value is determined by supply and demand.
A dividend is a payment made to shareholders from company profits.
Dividend yield is calculated by dividing the annual dividend by the market price.

quiz.say: A share has a market value of twenty units and pays a dividend of two units. What is the dividend yield?
quiz.why: The dividend yield is the dividend divided by the market value, so two divided by twenty equals zero point one.

wrong.0: This incorrectly adds the dividend and the market value together.
wrong.1: This incorrectly multiplies the two values together.
wrong.3: This incorrectly divides the dividend by the face value, ignoring the current market price.

quiz.say: If a share has a face value of five units but trades at a market value of fifty units, what is the face value?
quiz.why: The face value is the official, printed value set by the company, which is five units in this case.

wrong.1: This confuses the face value with the current market value.
wrong.2: This assumes all shares have a standard face value of one unit.
wrong.3: This incorrectly calculates the ratio between the two values.

quiz.say: A company pays a dividend of one unit. If the market price is five units, what is the dividend yield?
quiz.why: The dividend yield is the dividend payment divided by the current market price, which is one divided by five, equaling zero point two.

wrong.0: This incorrectly states the market value as the answer.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates the reciprocal, dividing five by one.
wrong.3: This incorrectly adds the dividend and the market value together.
